q: Which of these is NOT produced during the design development phase?
n: Technical/material specifications are typically finalized during the contract documents phase, while roof plans, ceiling plans, and floor plans are developed and refined earlier, in design development (Source: RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004), IRR – Scope of Architectural Practice (design phases)).
scenario:
A landowner intends to convert a rectangular, R-1-classified parcel with a total lot area of 1,934.72 square meters into an open-market residential subdivision within a built-up urban district. The development plan calls for six exclusive, semi-upscale housing units, each occupying a total lot allocation of 132.00 square meters, while every unit's enclosed floor space — its total gross floor area — is capped at 77.00 square meters; this 77.00 sqm figure counts only the roofed, enclosed portions of each house and does not include any additional floor area the owner might add later. Each individual house lot runs 12 meters deep.

The parcel is an interior lot (not a corner lot) and presents a 32.00-meter-wide frontage oriented toward the east. Across its length, the ground falls evenly at a 1% grade, with runoff draining toward the south. Fronting the property is a 15.00-meter-wide road right-of-way sitting at 0.00 elevation, flanked on both sides by a 1.80-meter paver-block sidewalk.

Cutting through the middle of the site along its long axis is an 8.00-meter-wide interior cluster street, meeting the main road right-of-way in a perpendicular intersection. This interior street climbs at a 10% grade running west to east — the same west-to-east direction the street itself follows — and it provides direct frontage to all ten house lots, five lined up on each side. The two outermost lots on the street's western end are each 31.45% larger in width than the lot sitting at the center of the row.

Guiding the design are four objectives: keep the project within R-1 zoning parameters; produce a tightly-planned residential enclave that can stand as a model development for the area; maximize the owner's financial return; and give the project a distinctive, landmark-quality presence in its surroundings.

q: In an R-1 development, on which sides of a lot may firewalls be built?
n: R-1 developments consist of single-detached houses, which by definition are freestanding with open space on all sides, so firewalls — shared party walls between adjoining units — do not apply.

A landowner intends to convert a rectangular, R-1-classified parcel with a total lot area of 1,934.72 square meters into an open-market residential subdivision within a built-up urban district. Each individual house lot runs 12 meters deep.

The parcel is an interior lot (not a corner lot) and presents a 32.00-meter-wide frontage oriented toward the east. This interior street climbs at a 10% grade running west to east — the same west-to-east direction the street itself follows — and it provides direct frontage to all ten house lots, five lined up on each side. The two outermost lots on the street's western end are each 31.45% larger in width than the lot sitting at the center of the row.

Guiding the design are four objectives: keep the project within R-1 zoning parameters; produce a tightly-planned residential enclave that can stand as a model development for the area; maximize the owner's financial return; and give the project a distinctive, landmark-quality presence in its surroundings.
